claim: SARS-CoV-2 antagonises the innate interferon response.
source: SARS-CoV-2 antagonises the innate interferon response, but whether it manipulates innate cellular immunity is unclear.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract, setting up the research question.

claim: An unbiased proteomic analysis determined how cell surface protein expression is altered on SARS-CoV-2-infected lung epithelial cells.
source: An unbiased proteomic analysis determined how cell surface protein expression is altered on SARS-CoV-2-infected lung epithelial cells, showing downregulation of activating NK ligands B7-H6, MICA, ULBP2, and Nectin1, with minimal effects on MHC-I.
evidence: The manuscript describes performing plasma membrane profiling (PMP) experiments and presents the resulting data.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection causes downregulation of activating NK ligands B7-H6, MICA, ULBP2, and Nectin1.
source: An unbiased proteomic analysis determined how cell surface protein expression is altered on SARS-CoV-2-infected lung epithelial cells, showing downregulation of activating NK ligands B7-H6, MICA, ULBP2, and Nectin1, with minimal effects on MHC-I.
evidence: This finding is supported by proteomic data shown in figures and confirmed by flow cytometry.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection has minimal effects on MHC-I expression.
source: An unbiased proteomic analysis determined how cell surface protein expression is altered on SARS-CoV-2-infected lung epithelial cells, showing downregulation of activating NK ligands B7-H6, MICA, ULBP2, and Nectin1, with minimal effects on MHC-I.
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data showing MHC-I proteins were upregulated in cluster 5 or unchanged.

claim: The downregulation of NK ligands occurred at the level of protein synthesis.
source: This occurred at the level of protein synthesis, could be mediated by Nsp1 and Nsp14, and correlated with a reduction in NK cell activation.
evidence: Biochemical experiments with EndoH digestion and proteasomal/lysosomal inhibitors support this mechanism.

claim: Nsp1 and Nsp14 can mediate the downregulation of NK ligands.
source: This occurred at the level of protein synthesis, could be mediated by Nsp1 and Nsp14, and correlated with a reduction in NK cell activation.
evidence: Transfection experiments with individual SARS-CoV-2 ORFs showed that Nsp1 and Nsp14 reduced NK ligand expression.

claim: The downregulation of NK ligands correlated with a reduction in NK cell activation.
source: This occurred at the level of protein synthesis, could be mediated by Nsp1 and Nsp14, and correlated with a reduction in NK cell activation.
evidence: Functional NK cell assays showed reduced degranulation and cytokine production against infected cells.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 host-shutoff antagonises innate immunity through a novel mechanism.
source: This identifies a novel mechanism by which SARS-CoV-2 host-shutoff antagonises innate immunity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings showing NK ligand downregulation via protein synthesis inhibition.

claim: Strong antibody-dependent NK cell activation (ADNKA) developed later in the disease process.
source: Later in the disease process, strong antibody-dependent NK cell activation (ADNKA) developed.
evidence: NK cell activation assays with sera from infected individuals showed strong ADNKA responses.

claim: ADNKA responses were sustained for at least 6 months in most patients.
source: These responses were sustained for at least 6 months in most patients, and led to high levels of pro-inflammatory cytokine production.
evidence: Longitudinal serum samples tested over 150-200 days showed persistent ADNKA activity.

claim: ADNKA responses led to high levels of pro-inflammatory cytokine production.
source: These responses were sustained for at least 6 months in most patients, and led to high levels of pro-inflammatory cytokine production.
evidence: NK cell assays measured TNFα and IFNγ production in response to infected cells with seropositive sera.

claim: Spike-specific antibodies play a dominant role in neutralisation.
source: Depletion of spike-specific antibodies confirmed their dominant role in neutralisation, but these antibodies played only a minor role in ADNKA compared to antibodies to other proteins, including ORF3a, Membrane, and Nucleocapsid.
evidence: Antibody depletion experiments showed loss of neutralization activity after spike antibody removal.

claim: Spike-specific antibodies play only a minor role in ADNKA compared to antibodies to other proteins.
source: Depletion of spike-specific antibodies confirmed their dominant role in neutralisation, but these antibodies played only a minor role in ADNKA compared to antibodies to other proteins, including ORF3a, Membrane, and Nucleocapsid.
evidence: Antibody depletion experiments showed no loss of ADNKA activity after spike antibody removal, but reduction after nucleocapsid depletion and ORF3a deletion.

claim: Antibodies to ORF3a, Membrane, and Nucleocapsid contribute to ADNKA.
source: Depletion of spike-specific antibodies confirmed their dominant role in neutralisation, but these antibodies played only a minor role in ADNKA compared to antibodies to other proteins, including ORF3a, Membrane, and Nucleocapsid.
evidence: Transfection experiments, antibody depletion, and virus deletion experiments demonstrated these proteins mediate ADNKA.

claim: ADNKA induced following vaccination was focused solely on spike.
source: In contrast, ADNKA induced following vaccination was focussed solely on spike, was weaker than ADNKA following natural infection, and was not boosted by the second dose.
evidence: Depletion of spike antibodies from vaccine sera eliminated ADNKA activity.

claim: ADNKA following vaccination was weaker than ADNKA following natural infection.
source: In contrast, ADNKA induced following vaccination was focussed solely on spike, was weaker than ADNKA following natural infection, and was not boosted by the second dose.
evidence: Comparison of AUC values for ADNKA between vaccinated and naturally infected individuals showed significantly lower responses in vaccinated individuals.

claim: ADNKA following vaccination was not boosted by the second dose.
source: In contrast, ADNKA induced following vaccination was focussed solely on spike, was weaker than ADNKA following natural infection, and was not boosted by the second dose.
evidence: Comparison of ADNKA responses after first and second vaccine doses showed no significant increase.

claim: NK cells bridge the innate and adaptive immune responses.
source: NK cells bridge the innate and adaptive responses, and individuals with NK cell deficiencies suffer severe viral infections (Orange, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Individuals with NK cell deficiencies suffer severe viral infections.
source: NK cells bridge the innate and adaptive responses, and individuals with NK cell deficiencies suffer severe viral infections (Orange, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Orange, 2013.

claim: Highly activated NK cells are seen in both the periphery and the lung in established COVID-19 infection.
source: The majority of studies on NK cells have focussed on their adaptive roles in established COVID-19 infection, with highly activated NK cells seen in both the periphery and the lung (Maucourant et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Maucourant et al., 2020.

claim: The genetic loss of NKG2C is a risk factor for severe COVID-19 disease.
source: The genetic loss of NKG2C (a hallmark of adaptive NK cells, capable of enhanced ADCC) is also a risk factor for severe disease (Vietzen et al., 2021b), implying a protective role in COVID-19 infection.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vietzen et al., 2021b.

claim: NKG2C is a hallmark of adaptive NK cells capable of enhanced ADCC.
source: The genetic loss of NKG2C (a hallmark of adaptive NK cells, capable of enhanced ADCC) is also a risk factor for severe disease (Vietzen et al., 2021b), implying a protective role in COVID-19 infection.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NK cell biology.

claim: NK cells have a protective role in COVID-19 infection.
source: The genetic loss of NKG2C (a hallmark of adaptive NK cells, capable of enhanced ADCC) is also a risk factor for severe disease (Vietzen et al., 2021b), implying a protective role in COVID-19 infection.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that loss of NKG2C increases disease severity.

claim: Fc-mediated functions correlate with protection in animal models of SARS-CoV-2 vaccination.
source: In support of this, in animal models, Fc-mediated functions correlate with protection in vaccination (Gorman et al., 2021), and monoclonal antibody-mediated control of SARS-CoV-2 infection is enhanced by Fc-dependent mechanisms (Chan et al., 2020; Schäfer et al., 2021; Winkler et al., 2020; Suryadevara et al., 2021; Winkler et al., 2021; Yamin et al., 2021), which enable control of disease even in the absence of neutralising activity (Beaudoin-Bussières et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gorman et al., 2021.

claim: Monoclonal antibody-mediated control of SARS-CoV-2 infection is enhanced by Fc-dependent mechanisms.
source: In support of this, in animal models, Fc-mediated functions correlate with protection in vaccination (Gorman et al., 2021), and monoclonal antibody-mediated control of SARS-CoV-2 infection is enhanced by Fc-dependent mechanisms (Chan et al., 2020; Schäfer et al., 2021; Winkler et al., 2020; Suryadevara et al., 2021; Winkler et al., 2021; Yamin et al., 2021), which enable control of disease even in the absence of neutralising activity (Beaudoin-Bussières et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to animal studies.

claim: Fc-dependent mechanisms enable control of SARS-CoV-2 disease even in the absence of neutralising activity.
source: In support of this, in animal models, Fc-mediated functions correlate with protection in vaccination (Gorman et al., 2021), and monoclonal antibody-mediated control of SARS-CoV-2 infection is enhanced by Fc-dependent mechanisms (Chan et al., 2020; Schäfer et al., 2021; Winkler et al., 2020; Suryadevara et al., 2021; Winkler et al., 2021; Yamin et al., 2021), which enable control of disease even in the absence of neutralising activity (Beaudoin-Bussières et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Beaudoin-Bussières et al., 2021.

claim: Fc-activity is required for efficacy when neutralising monoclonal antibodies are administered therapeutically to animals.
source: Furthermore, although neutralising monoclonal antibodies are effective when administered prophylactically, Fc-activity is required for efficacy when administered to animals therapeutically (Yamin et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yamin et al., 2021.

claim: Previous studies have assumed spike protein is the dominant ADCC target.
source: Studies to date have assumed spike protein is the dominant ADCC target, and have tested plate-bound protein or transfected cells (Barrett et al., 2021; Herman et al., 2021; Zohar et al., 2020; Tauzin et al., 2021; Anand et al., 2021; Lee et al., 2020; Dufloo et al., 2020; Tortorici et al., 2020; McCallum et al., 2021; Cathcart et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: ADNKA-inducing antibodies are generated following SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: Using these systems, they have shown that ADNKA-inducing antibodies are generated following SARS-CoV-2 infection (Herman et al., 2021; Anand et al., 2021; Lee et al., 2020; Dufloo et al., 2020), are induced by vaccination in humans (Barrett et al., 2021; Tauzin et al., 2021), and can be mediated by a subset of neutralising monoclonal antibodies targeting the spike protein (Tortorici et al., 2020; McCallum et al., 2021; Cathcart et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ADNKA-inducing antibodies are induced by vaccination in humans.
source: Using these systems, they have shown that ADNKA-inducing antibodies are generated following SARS-CoV-2 infection (Herman et al., 2021; Anand et al., 2021; Lee et al., 2020; Dufloo et al., 2020), are induced by vaccination in humans (Barrett et al., 2021; Tauzin et al., 2021), and can be mediated by a subset of neutralising monoclonal antibodies targeting the spike protein (Tortorici et al., 2020; McCallum et al., 2021; Cathcart et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Barrett et al., 2021 and Tauzin et al., 2021.

claim: ADNKA can be mediated by a subset of neutralising monoclonal antibodies targeting the spike protein.
source: Using these systems, they have shown that ADNKA-inducing antibodies are generated following SARS-CoV-2 infection (Herman et al., 2021; Anand et al., 2021; Lee et al., 2020; Dufloo et al., 2020), are induced by vaccination in humans (Barrett et al., 2021; Tauzin et al., 2021), and can be mediated by a subset of neutralising monoclonal antibodies targeting the spike protein (Tortorici et al., 2020; McCallum et al., 2021; Cathcart et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Previous ADCC studies have not been tested against SARS-CoV-2 infected cells.
source: However, these responses have not been tested against SARS-CoV-2 infected cells; the presence, abundance, accessibility, and conformation of viral glycoproteins can be very different during productive infection.
evidence: This is a critical observation about the limitations of previous studies.

claim: The presence, abundance, accessibility, and conformation of viral glycoproteins can be very different during productive infection compared to transfected cells.
source: However, these responses have not been tested against SARS-CoV-2 infected cells; the presence, abundance, accessibility, and conformation of viral glycoproteins can be very different during productive infection.
evidence: This is established knowledge about viral protein expression.

claim: Non-structural proteins are often the dominant targets of ADCC in other viruses.
source: Furthermore, although viral entry glycoproteins such as spike can be found on the infected cell surface, and can mediate ADCC, other viral proteins can be the dominant mediators of ADCC during infection; indeed, we have shown that in other viruses, non-structural proteins are often the dominant targets (Vlahava et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work on HCMV.

claim: Successful viruses must counteract robust NK activation to establish infection.
source: In addition, there is little information on the NK cell response to SARS-CoV-2 infected cells during the innate phase of infection, despite this process being important to virus pathogenesis; successful viruses must counteract robust NK activation to establish infection, and their ability to do this is critical to their ability to cause disease (Patel et al., 2018; Berry et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: NK cell activation depends on the balance of ligands for a wide range of inhibitory or activating receptors.
source: NK cell activation is complex and depends on the balance of ligands for a wide range of inhibitory or activating receptors (Kumar, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: MICA, MICB, and ULBP1-6 are stress ligands that bind to the activating receptor NKG2D.
source: For example, the stress ligands MICA, MICB, and ULBP1-6, all bind to the ubiquitously expressed activating receptor NKG2D.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NK cell biology.

claim: Many viruses manipulate NK activating ligands to limit NK cell activation.
source: To limit NK cell activation, many viruses manipulate these NK activating ligands, reducing NK-cell-mediated control (Patel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: A549-ACE2-TMPRSS2 (AAT) cells are highly permissive to SARS-CoV-2.
source: We therefore applied PMP to SARS-CoV-2 infected A549-ACE2-TMPRSS2 (AAT) cells, which are highly permissive to SARS-CoV-2 (Rihn et al., 2021) and infection at a high multiplicity of infection (MOI) results in over 90% infection by 24 hr (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Infection of AAT cells at high MOI results in over 90% infection by 24 hours.
source: We therefore applied PMP to SARS-CoV-2 infected A549-ACE2-TMPRSS2 (AAT) cells, which are highly permissive to SARS-CoV-2 (Rihn et al., 2021) and infection at a high multiplicity of infection (MOI) results in over 90% infection by 24 hr (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 1A.

claim: 4953 proteins were quantitated in the PMP analysis.
source: In total, 4953 proteins were quantitated, including 2227 proteins with gene ontology annotation associated with the cell surface and plasma membrane (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a direct result from the proteomic analysis.

claim: 2227 proteins with gene ontology annotation associated with the cell surface and plasma membrane were quantitated.
source: In total, 4953 proteins were quantitated, including 2227 proteins with gene ontology annotation associated with the cell surface and plasma membrane (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Plasma membrane annotated proteins made up nearly 80% of the total protein abundance.
source: Importantly however, the plasma membrane annotated proteins made up nearly 80% of the total protein abundance, indicating a high degree of enrichment for plasma membrane proteins, comparable with our previous PMP datasets (Vlahava et al., 2021; Weekes et al., 2010; Weekes et al., 2014; Matheson et al., 2015; Fielding et al., 2017; Hsu et al., 2015; Weekes et al., 2013; Soh et al., 2020).
evidence: This is calculated from the proteomic data and compared to previous studies.

claim: Five SARS-CoV-2 viral proteins were detected in the PMP analysis.
source: Five SARS-CoV-2 viral proteins were detected (see later), including spike, ORF3A, and membrane, which have previously been annotated as having a cell surface localisation (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a result from the proteomic analysis.

claim: Spike, ORF3A, and membrane have previously been annotated as having a cell surface localisation.
source: Five SARS-CoV-2 viral proteins were detected (see later), including spike, ORF3A, and membrane, which have previously been annotated as having a cell surface localisation (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is established knowledge about these viral proteins.

claim: The viral receptor ACE2 was strongly downregulated after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: Consistent with prior reports, the viral receptor ACE2 was strongly downregulated after infection (Patra et al., 2020), while TMPRSS2 expression was unaffected (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown in the proteomic data and supported by a citation.

claim: TMPRSS2 expression was unaffected by SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: Consistent with prior reports, the viral receptor ACE2 was strongly downregulated after infection (Patra et al., 2020), while TMPRSS2 expression was unaffected (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown in the proteomic data in Figure 1C.

claim: 914 plasma membrane proteins showed significant changes with greater than 1.5-fold alteration over the time course.
source: Overall, of the 2227 PM proteins quantified with more than one peptide, 914 showed changes which were both significant and with a greater than 1.5-fold alteration over the course of the experiment.
evidence: This is a result from statistical analysis of the proteomic data.

claim: K-means clustering defined five groups of significantly altered proteins by their temporal profile.
source: Here, we used K-means clustering to define five groups of significantly altered proteins by their temporal profile.
evidence: This is the analytical approach used and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Thirteen of the 23 detected plasma membrane genes associated with the interferon response fell into cluster 5.
source: Thirteen of the 23 detected PM genes associated with the interferon response fell into cluster 5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, Supplementary file 2), which describes proteins with an increase in expression at 48 hr, examples shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.
evidence: This is shown in the supplementary figure and data file.

claim: The SARS-CoV-2 viral replication cycle is completed in less than 24 hours.
source: As the SARS-CoV-2 viral replication cycle is completed in less than 24 hr (Lei et al., 2020), SARS-CoV-2 is able to evade innate immune recognition and/or suppress IFN signalling until long after virus egress has been achieved.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lei et al., 2020.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 is able to evade innate immune recognition and/or suppress IFN signalling until long after virus egress.
source: As the SARS-CoV-2 viral replication cycle is completed in less than 24 hr (Lei et al., 2020), SARS-CoV-2 is able to evade innate immune recognition and/or suppress IFN signalling until long after virus egress has been achieved.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that interferon-stimulated genes are only upregulated at 48 hours.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection results in downregulation of IFNAR1 at the plasma membrane.
source: Several classifications enriched in this cluster are particularly relevant, including the downregulation of several cytokine receptors, including IFNAR1. Much of the SARS-CoV-2 genome is dedicated to antagonising a type I interferon response within an infected cell (Lei et al., 2020) and the plasma membrane downregulation of IFNAR1 presents a previously undescribed strategy to prevent signalling from exogenous IFN.
evidence: This is shown in the proteomic data and pathway analysis.

claim: Plasma membrane downregulation of IFNAR1 presents a previously undescribed strategy to prevent signalling from exogenous IFN.
source: Much of the SARS-CoV-2 genome is dedicated to antagonising a type I interferon response within an infected cell (Lei et al., 2020) and the plasma membrane downregulation of IFNAR1 presents a previously undescribed strategy to prevent signalling from exogenous IFN.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the novel finding of IFNAR1 downregulation.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection results in downregulation of heparan sulfate proteoglycans.
source: Also of note is the downregulation of heparan sulfate proteoglycans, the syndecan (SDC), glypican (GPC), and neurophillin (NRP) proteins, which together encompass the families of heparan sulfate modified proteins expressed on epithelial cells (Sarrazin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is shown in the proteomic data and pathway analysis.

claim: NRP1 is a cell entry factor for SARS-CoV-2.
source: NRP1 is a cell entry factor for SARS-CoV-2 (Cantuti-Castelvetri et al., 2020; Daly et al., 2020), and SARS-CoV-2 spike is also reported to bind heparan sulphated proteins (Clausen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 spike binds heparan sulphated proteins.
source: NRP1 is a cell entry factor for SARS-CoV-2 (Cantuti-Castelvetri et al., 2020; Daly et al., 2020), and SARS-CoV-2 spike is also reported to bind heparan sulphated proteins (Clausen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Clausen et al., 2020.

claim: The decrease in cell surface expression of heparan sulfated proteins may enable egress of viral particles and prevent super-infection.
source: The decrease in cell surface expression of heparan sulfated proteins may therefore enable the egress of viral particles and prevent super-infection, and is reminiscent of the capacity of other viruses to downregulate both primary viral receptors and co-receptors (Landi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed downregulation and comparison to other viruses.

claim: 18 NK ligands were detected in the PMP dataset.
source: As these ligands are poorly annotated in public databases, we investigated the PMP dataset for previously described ligands (Kumar, 2018), of which 18 were detected (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: MHC-I proteins HLA-B to HLA-E were upregulated in cluster 5.
source: MHC-I proteins HLA-B to HLA-E were upregulated in cluster 5, likely reflecting a late IFN-mediated upregulation, while HLA-A was unchanged.
evidence: This is shown in the proteomic data.

claim: HLA-A expression was unchanged by SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: MHC-I proteins HLA-B to HLA-E were upregulated in cluster 5, likely reflecting a late IFN-mediated upregulation, while HLA-A was unchanged.
evidence: This is shown in the proteomic data.

claim: The upregulation of MHC-I proteins likely reflects a late IFN-mediated upregulation.
source: MHC-I proteins HLA-B to HLA-E were upregulated in cluster 5, likely reflecting a late IFN-mediated upregulation, while HLA-A was unchanged.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the timing and known IFN effects.

claim: The activating NK-cell ligands MICA, ULBP2, B7-H6, and Nectin1 were significantly downregulated in cluster 1.
source: By contrast, the activating NK-cell ligands MICA, ULBP2, B7-H6 (NCR3LG1), and Nectin1 (which is inhibitory in mice, but recently reported as activating in humans Holmes, 2019) were significantly downregulated in cluster 1.
evidence: This is shown in the proteomic data.

claim: Nectin1 is inhibitory in mice but activating in humans.
source: By contrast, the activating NK-cell ligands MICA, ULBP2, B7-H6 (NCR3LG1), and Nectin1 (which is inhibitory in mice, but recently reported as activating in humans Holmes, 2019) were significantly downregulated in cluster 1.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Holmes, 2019.

claim: The downregulation of NK ligands was confirmed by flow cytometry in multiple cell types.
source: This was confirmed by flow cytometry in multiple cell types (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Flow cytometry data is shown in the figures.

claim: The downregulation of NK ligands was dependent on virus replication.
source: These responses were dependent on virus replication, because no alterations in ligand abundance were observed when virus was heat-inactivated (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is shown by comparing active and heat-inactivated virus in the supplementary figure.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection does not result in intracellular retention of NK ligands.
source: Following infection with SARS-CoV-2, levels of all three NK ligands were substantially reduced, however there was no alteration in the pattern of EndoH sensitivity (Figure 3B). Thus, SARS-CoV-2 infection does not result in intracellular retention of NK ligands, but instead reduces the overall abundance of protein.
evidence: This is demonstrated by EndoH digestion experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection reduces the overall abundance of NK ligand protein.
source: Following infection with SARS-CoV-2, levels of all three NK ligands were substantially reduced, however there was no alteration in the pattern of EndoH sensitivity (Figure 3B). Thus, SARS-CoV-2 infection does not result in intracellular retention of NK ligands, but instead reduces the overall abundance of protein.
evidence: This is shown by western blot analysis in Figure 3B.

claim: MG132 did not result in recovery of NK ligand levels during SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: When tested with overexpressed MICA or B7-H6 (ULBP2 was not tested), MG132 did not result in recovery of NK ligand levels.
evidence: This is shown by western blot analysis in Figure 3C.

claim: Leupeptin resulted in a small recovery of B7-H6 in both mock and infected cells.
source: Leupeptin resulted in a small recovery of B7-H6; however, this was seen in both Mock and infected cells, implying that it reflects constitutive turnover of the ligand rather than virus-specific targeting, and recovery in infected cells remained reduced compared to untreated mock infected cells.
evidence: This is shown by western blot analysis in Figure 3C.

claim: The virus targets NK ligands at the level of synthesis rather than post-translationally.
source: Overall, these results are consistent with the virus targeting NK ligands at the level of synthesis, rather than post-translationally.
evidence: This is inferred from the EndoH and inhibitor experiments.

claim: Cycloheximide treatment resulted in rapid loss of MICA, ULBP2, and B7-H6, but not GFP.
source: This resulted in rapid loss of MICA, ULBP2, and B7-H6, but not GFP (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown by western blot analysis in Figure 4A.

claim: Only Nsp1 and Nsp14 resulted in a reduction of NK ligand staining when SARS-CoV-2 ORFs were transfected individually.
source: Finally, to determine which viral proteins were responsible for these effects, we transfected cells with a library of previously validated plasmids expressing all 29 SARS-CoV-2 ORFs individually (Gordon et al., 2020), and assessed them for levels of NK ligands on the cell surface. Only two SARS-CoV-2 ORFs resulted in a reduction of staining; Nsp1 and Nsp14 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry analysis in Figure 4B.

claim: For MICA and ULBP2, Nsp14 consistently resulted in the strongest reduction.
source: For MICA and ULBP2, Nsp14 consistently resulted in the strongest reduction, with Nsp1 being weaker.
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry analysis in Figure 4B.

claim: For Nectin1 and B7-H6, both Nsp1 and Nsp14 resulted in similar reductions.
source: For Nectin1 and B7-H6, effects were weaker, but both Nsp1 and Nsp14 resulted in similar reductions.
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry analysis in Figure 4B.

claim: Both Nsp1 and Nsp14 are involved in the ability of SARS-CoV-2 to degrade host RNA and inhibit host protein translation.
source: Both Nsp1 and Nsp14 are involved in the ability of SARS-CoV-2 to degrade host RNA (Nsp1), and inhibit host protein translation (Nsp1 and Nsp14), and these activities have been implicated in their ability to counteract the interferon response within the infected cell (Yuan et al., 2021; Hsu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yuan et al., 2021 and Hsu et al., 2021.

claim: NK ligands are highly susceptible to inhibition of synthesis.
source: Together with our biochemical analysis, this data suggests that NK ligands are highly susceptible to inhibition of synthesis, and that SARS-CoV-2 manipulation of host protein production could impact the NK response in addition to the interferon response.
evidence: This is inferred from the cycloheximide and Nsp1/Nsp14 experiments.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 manipulation of host protein production could impact the NK response in addition to the interferon response.
source: Together with our biochemical analysis, this data suggests that NK ligands are highly susceptible to inhibition of synthesis, and that SARS-CoV-2 manipulation of host protein production could impact the NK response in addition to the interferon response.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined biochemical and functional data.

claim: Degranulation of CD3-CD56+ NK cells was significantly reduced against SARS-CoV-2 infected cells.
source: To determine whether this was the case, we incubated SARS-CoV-2 infected cells with PBMC, and measured (i) degranulation of CD3-CD56+ NK cells (Figure 4C; Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), (ii) production of IFNγ (Figure 4D), and (iii) TNFα (Figure 4E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B). Consistent with data using other viruses Vlahava et al., 2021, CD107a was recirculated on a higher proportion of NK cells than IFNγ and TNFα. Nevertheless, all three markers of NK activation were significantly reduced in SARS-CoV-2 infected versus mock infected cells, suggesting that the virus has evolved to inhibit NK cell responses.
evidence: This is shown by functional NK cell assays in Figures 4C-E.

claim: Production of IFNγ by NK cells was significantly reduced against SARS-CoV-2 infected cells.
source: To determine whether this was the case, we incubated SARS-CoV-2 infected cells with PBMC, and measured (i) degranulation of CD3-CD56+ NK cells (Figure 4C; Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), (ii) production of IFNγ (Figure 4D), and (iii) TNFα (Figure 4E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B). Consistent with data using other viruses Vlahava et al., 2021, CD107a was recirculated on a higher proportion of NK cells than IFNγ and TNFα. Nevertheless, all three markers of NK activation were significantly reduced in SARS-CoV-2 infected versus mock infected cells, suggesting that the virus has evolved to inhibit NK cell responses.
evidence: This is shown by functional NK cell assays in Figure 4D.

claim: Production of TNFα by NK cells was significantly reduced against SARS-CoV-2 infected cells.
source: To determine whether this was the case, we incubated SARS-CoV-2 infected cells with PBMC, and measured (i) degranulation of CD3-CD56+ NK cells (Figure 4C; Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), (ii) production of IFNγ (Figure 4D), and (iii) TNFα (Figure 4E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B). Consistent with data using other viruses Vlahava et al., 2021, CD107a was recirculated on a higher proportion of NK cells than IFNγ and TNFα. Nevertheless, all three markers of NK activation were significantly reduced in SARS-CoV-2 infected versus mock infected cells, suggesting that the virus has evolved to inhibit NK cell responses.
evidence: This is shown by functional NK cell assays in Figure 4E.

claim: CD107a was recirculated on a higher proportion of NK cells than IFNγ and TNFα.
source: Consistent with data using other viruses Vlahava et al., 2021, CD107a was recirculated on a higher proportion of NK cells than IFNγ and TNFα.
evidence: This is observed in the data and consistent with previous studies.

claim: The virus has evolved to inhibit NK cell responses.
source: Nevertheless, all three markers of NK activation were significantly reduced in SARS-CoV-2 infected versus mock infected cells, suggesting that the virus has evolved to inhibit NK cell responses.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional NK cell data.

claim: Degranulation, IFNγ production, and TNFα production were all significantly increased in the presence of serum containing anti-SARS-CoV-2 antibodies.
source: Degranulation (Figure 5A), as well as production of IFNγ (Figure 5B) and TNFα (Figure 5C), were all significantly increased in the presence of serum containing anti-SARS-CoV-2 antibodies, across a range of different NK donors (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: This is shown by functional NK cell assays in Figures 5A-F.

claim: ADNKA was dependent on virus replication.
source: ADNKA was dependent on virus replication, since heat inactivated virus did not lead to serum-dependent NK degranulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown by comparing active and heat-inactivated virus in the supplementary figure.

claim: NK cells were activated equivalently whether purified NK cells or PBMC were used.
source: NK cells were activated equivalently whether purified NK cells or PBMC were used (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), thus these responses are due to direct stimulation of NK cells, rather than other cells responding to antibodies and releasing NK stimulating cytokines.
evidence: This is shown by comparing PBMC and purified NK cells in the supplementary figure.

claim: ADNKA responses are due to direct stimulation of NK cells.
source: NK cells were activated equivalently whether purified NK cells or PBMC were used (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), thus these responses are due to direct stimulation of NK cells, rather than other cells responding to antibodies and releasing NK stimulating cytokines.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of PBMC and purified NK cells.

claim: Viral immune evasion can be overcome through antibody dependent mechanisms.
source: Viral immune evasion can therefore be overcome through antibody dependent mechanisms, suggesting that in addition to neutralising virus, SARS-CoV-2 antibodies may aid virus clearance through ADCC.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ADNKA is strong despite NK ligand downregulation.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 antibodies may aid virus clearance through ADCC.
source: Viral immune evasion can therefore be overcome through antibody dependent mechanisms, suggesting that in addition to neutralising virus, SARS-CoV-2 antibodies may aid virus clearance through ADCC.
evidence: This is speculation based on the strong ADNKA responses observed.

claim: The magnitude of the neutralising antibody response to SARS-CoV-2 correlates with severity of disease.
source: The magnitude of the neutralising antibody response to SARS-CoV-2 correlates with severity of disease; individuals with more severe disease generate higher levels of neutralising antibody (Seow et al., 2020; Dan et al., 2021; Wajnberg et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Levels of circulating antibody can decrease over time following resolution of disease.
source: Although memory B-cell responses persist, levels of circulating antibody can decrease over time following resolution of disease, such that in some mildly infected people they become undetectable after a few months (Seow et al., 2020; Dan et al., 2021; Wajnberg et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ADNKA responses were generally of greater magnitude in individuals with more severe disease.
source: ADNKA responses were generally of greater magnitude in individuals with more severe disease, with responses remaining detectable during the 150–200 day follow-up.
evidence: This is shown by longitudinal serum analysis in Figure 5G.

claim: Strong initial ADNKA responses were maintained over time in individuals with milder disease.
source: Amongst those with milder disease, strong initial responses were maintained over time, while weaker responses decreased, becoming virtually undetectable by around 200 days.
evidence: This is shown by longitudinal serum analysis in Figure 5G.

claim: Weaker ADNKA responses decreased in individuals with milder disease, becoming virtually undetectable by around 200 days.
source: Amongst those with milder disease, strong initial responses were maintained over time, while weaker responses decreased, becoming virtually undetectable by around 200 days.
evidence: This is shown by longitudinal serum analysis in Figure 5G.

claim: There was a moderate correlation between the ability of antibodies to neutralise SARS-CoV-2 and to activate ADNKA.
source: There was a moderate correlation between the ability of antibodies to neutralise SARS-CoV-2, and to activate ADNKA in response to SARS-CoV-2 (Figure 5H), with a R2 value of 0.7.
evidence: This is shown by correlation analysis in Figure 5H.

claim: The antibodies mediating neutralisation and ADNKA may not be identical.
source: Thus, although the antibodies mediating these activities may be induced in a similar manner, the antibodies mediating the two responses may not be identical.
evidence: This is inferred from the moderate (not perfect) correlation between neutralisation and ADNKA.

claim: Substantial levels of spike protein were detected on the infected cell surface by PMP and flow cytometry.
source: It is certainly a potential target during infection as, despite the fact that virion particles bud internally rather than from the cell membrane, both our PMP and flow cytometric analysis detected substantial levels of spike protein on the infected cell surface (Figure 6A, C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is shown by proteomic and flow cytometry data in the figures.

claim: PMP detected membrane (M), nucleocapsid (N), ORF3a, and ORF1ab on the cell surface.
source: However, our studies with other viruses have demonstrated that although viral proteins involved in virion binding and entry are found on the cell surface, and can be bound by antibody, they are not necessarily the strongest mediators of ADCC activity (Vlahava et al., 2021). PMP also detected membrane (M), nucleocapsid (N), ORF3a, and ORF1ab on the cell surface.
evidence: This is shown by the proteomic data.

claim: ORF1ab was only present at very low levels (1% of all viral proteins) in PMP.
source: Furthermore, comparing the relative abundance of viral proteins in PMP, ORF1ab was only present at very low levels (1% of all viral proteins, significantly lower than any other SARS-CoV-2 protein).
evidence: This is calculated from the proteomic data.

claim: It is unlikely that any NSPs are surface-exposed.
source: Taken together, it is unlikely that any NSPs are surface-exposed.
evidence: This is inferred from the low abundance of ORF1ab and lack of specific NSP enrichment.

claim: Bioinformatic analysis revealed five additional candidate cell-surface proteins: Nsp4, Nsp6, ORF6, ORF7a, ORF7b.
source: Nevertheless, we performed bioinformatic analysis of all viral proteins for the presence of potential transmembrane domains or signal peptides, revealing five additional candidate cell-surface proteins (Nsp4, Nsp6, ORF6, ORF7a, ORF7b).
evidence: This is the result of bioinformatic analysis.

claim: Spike primed a substantial ADNKA response when transfected into cells.
source: As expected, spike primed a substantial ADNKA response.
evidence: This is shown by functional NK cell assays in Figure 6B.

claim: Expression of ORF3a, membrane, and nucleocapsid were capable of priming ADNKA in the presence of serum containing SARS-CoV-2 antibodies.
source: However, in support of our PMP data, expression of ORF3a, membrane, and nucleocapsid, were also capable of priming ADNKA in the presence of serum containing SARS-CoV-2 antibodies, while the Nsps did not.
evidence: This is shown by functional NK cell assays in Figure 6B.

claim: The Nsps did not prime ADNKA.
source: However, in support of our PMP data, expression of ORF3a, membrane, and nucleocapsid, were also capable of priming ADNKA in the presence of serum containing SARS-CoV-2 antibodies, while the Nsps did not.
evidence: This is shown by functional NK cell assays in Figure 6B.

claim: Nucleocapsid has previously been assumed to be intracellular.
source: Interestingly, nucleocapsid readily activated ADNKA despite the fact that this protein has previously been assumed to be intracellular.
evidence: This is established knowledge that is being challenged by the current findings.

claim: ADNKA can be activated in response to levels of virus protein that are difficult to detect by flow cytometry.
source: We have previously observed the exquisite sensitivity of ADNKA, which can be activated in response to levels of virus protein that are difficult to detect by flow cytometry (Vlahava et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Antigen levels can be very different in the context of virus infection compared with transfection.
source: We have also shown that antigen levels can be very different in the context of virus infection, compared with transfection (Vlahava et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Nucleocapsid levels were much higher on the surface of infected cells than transfected cells.
source: In support of this, nucleocapsid levels were much higher on the surface of infected cells than transfected cells (Figure 6C); detection of nucleocapsid was dependent on virus replication (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), and occurred following infection of multiple different cell types (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry in Figure 6C and supplementary figures.

claim: Detection of nucleocapsid on the cell surface was dependent on virus replication.
source: In support of this, nucleocapsid levels were much higher on the surface of infected cells than transfected cells (Figure 6C); detection of nucleocapsid was dependent on virus replication (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), and occurred following infection of multiple different cell types (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown by comparing active and heat-inactivated virus in the supplementary figure.

claim: Nucleocapsid was detected on the cell surface following infection of multiple different cell types.
source: In support of this, nucleocapsid levels were much higher on the surface of infected cells than transfected cells (Figure 6C); detection of nucleocapsid was dependent on virus replication (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), and occurred following infection of multiple different cell types (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry of different cell types in the supplementary figure.

claim: The presence of nucleocapsid on the cell surface was supported by immunofluorescence staining of non-permeabilised infected cells.
source: The presence of nucleocapsid on the cell surface was also supported by immunofluorescence staining of non-permeabilised infected cells (Figure 6D), where distinct patches of nucleocapsid were observed that sometimes, but not always, coincided with cell-cell junctions.
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence microscopy in Figure 6D.

claim: Multiple proteins could be major contributors to ADCC during SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: Given how well even very low levels of surface nucleocapsid activated ADNKA, this suggested that multiple proteins could be major contributors to ADCC during SARS-CoV-2 infection.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional data showing multiple proteins can activate ADNKA.

claim: A panel of 26 human anti-spike monoclonal antibodies was tested, including antibodies targeting the RBD, S1, NTD, and S2 domains.
source: To determine the relative contribution of spike, and of different antigenic sites on spike, to ADNKA during SARS-CoV-2 infection, we tested a panel of 26 human anti-spike monoclonal antibodies, which had been isolated from naturally infected donors, and cloned as IgG1 constructs (Graham et al., 2021). The panel included antibodies targeting the RBD, S1, NTD, and S2 domains, neutralising and non-neutralising, and those targeting multiple distinct epitopes (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach and is supported by a citation.

claim: All 26 anti-spike antibodies bound efficiently to infected cells.
source: All 26 antibodies bound efficiently to infected cells, at levels comparable to polyclonal serum (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry in the supplementary figure.

claim: Only five of 26 anti-spike antibodies were capable of triggering NK cell degranulation.
source: However, only five of these antibodies were capable of triggering degranulation (Figure 7A), of which two triggered TNFα (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A), and one IFNγ (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is shown by functional NK cell assays in Figure 7A and supplementary figures.

claim: NK responses to anti-spike monoclonal antibodies were at dramatically lower levels than seen with polyclonal serum from a naturally infected donor.
source: Importantly, these NK responses were at dramatically lower levels than seen with polyclonal serum from a naturally infected donor, even when combined (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is shown by comparing monoclonal antibodies to polyclonal serum in Figure 7B.

claim: mAbs that induced ADNKA against infected cells also induced ADNKA against transfected cells.
source: mAbs that induced ADNKA against infected cells also induced ADNKA against transfected cells (P008-014 and P054-044).
evidence: This is shown by comparing infected and transfected cells in Figure 7C.

claim: Of 12 antibodies that failed to activate ADNKA against infected cells, 5 induced potent ADNKA against transfected cells.
source: However, of 12 antibodies that failed to activate ADNKA against infected cells, 5 induced potent ADNKA against transfected cells.
evidence: This is shown by comparing infected and transfected cells in Figure 7C.

claim: The level of ADNKA induced by mAbs was extremely high against transfected cells, with many exceeding that of control seropositive serum.
source: Furthermore, in contrast to infected cells, the level of ADNKA induced by mAbs was extremely high against transfected cells, with many exceeding that of our control seropositive serum.
evidence: This is shown by comparing monoclonal antibodies to polyclonal serum against transfected cells in Figure 7C.

claim: Spike was a relatively poor ADCC target in the context of natural infection when using mAbs.
source: Thus, despite a substantial ability to activate ADCC against cells transfected with spike protein, and high levels of antibody binding, spike was a relatively poor ADCC target in the context of natural infection when using mAbs.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of infected and transfected cells.

claim: ELISA analysis confirmed the effective depletion of spike-specific antibodies from naturally infected sera.
source: ELISA analysis confirmed the effective depletion of spike-specific antibodies (Figure 8A), which was accompanied by a significant loss of neutralisation activity (Figure 8B), across multiple donors (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is shown by ELISA in Figure 8A.

claim: Depletion of spike-specific antibodies was accompanied by a significant loss of neutralisation activity.
source: ELISA analysis confirmed the effective depletion of spike-specific antibodies (Figure 8A), which was accompanied by a significant loss of neutralisation activity (Figure 8B), across multiple donors (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is shown by neutralisation assays in Figures 8B and 8C.

claim: There was no loss of ADNKA activity following spike-antibody depletion from naturally infected sera.
source: However, there was no loss of ADNKA activity from any of these samples following spike-antibody depletion (Figure 8D and E), consistent with the results of our monoclonal antibody data.
evidence: This is shown by ADNKA assays in Figures 8D and 8E.

claim: Spike-specific antibodies dominate the neutralising antibody response but play minor roles in the ADCC response following natural infection.
source: We conclude that spike-specific antibodies dominate the neutralising antibody response, but play a minor roles in the ADCC response following natural infection.
evidence: This is the conclusion drawn from the antibody depletion experiments.

claim: A nucleocapsid-specific human monoclonal antibody was capable of activating ADNKA against infected cells.
source: A nucleocapsid-specific human monoclonal antibody was capable of activating ADNKA against infected cells (Figure 8F) and, although not to the extent of polyclonal serum, was superior to our best anti-spike antibody.
evidence: This is shown by functional NK cell assays in Figure 8F.

claim: The nucleocapsid-specific monoclonal antibody was superior to the best anti-spike antibody at activating ADNKA.
source: A nucleocapsid-specific human monoclonal antibody was capable of activating ADNKA against infected cells (Figure 8F) and, although not to the extent of polyclonal serum, was superior to our best anti-spike antibody.
evidence: This is shown by comparing the nucleocapsid and spike antibodies in Figure 8F.

claim: Depletion of both spike and nucleocapsid antibodies resulted in a significant reduction in ADNKA activity.
source: Furthermore, when we used the serums from which Spike antibodies had been depleted (Figure 8D–E), and also depleted anti-nucleocapsid antibodies, we saw a significant reduction in ADNKA activity (Figure 8G–H), although considerable activity remained.
evidence: This is shown by ADNKA assays in Figures 8G and 8H.

claim: Considerable ADNKA activity remained after depletion of both spike and nucleocapsid antibodies.
source: Furthermore, when we used the serums from which Spike antibodies had been depleted (Figure 8D–E), and also depleted anti-nucleocapsid antibodies, we saw a significant reduction in ADNKA activity (Figure 8G–H), although considerable activity remained.
evidence: This is shown by ADNKA assays in Figures 8G and 8H.

claim: Deletion of ORF3a resulted in a small reduction (~1 log) in virus titres.
source: Reagents are not available to deplete antibodies targeting ORF3a or membrane, so we instead deleted ORF3a from the virus genome. In line with existing data, this resulted in a small reduction (~1 log) in virus titres (not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments.

claim: Deletion of ORF3a resulted in a small reduction in levels of spike and nucleocapsid, but not membrane.
source: We therefore assessed levels of viral antigens on the cell surface following infection, which revealed that deletion of ORF3a resulted in a small reduction in levels of spike and nucleocapsid, but not membrane (Figure 8I).
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry in Figure 8I.

claim: Deletion of ORF3a resulted in a dramatic reduction in ADNKA activity when using sera depleted of spike and nucleocapsid antibodies.
source: To ensure that these alterations did not affect readouts, we used serums that had been depleted for antibodies targeting both Spike and Nucleocapsid, and compared ADNKA responses against wildtype or ΔORF3a virus (Figure 8J–K). Deletion of ORF3a resulted in a dramatic reduction in ADNKA activity, although this was not reduced completely to the level of seronegative serum.
evidence: This is shown by ADNKA assays in Figures 8J and 8K.

claim: Nucleocapsid and ORF3a are targets for ADNKA activity against SARS-CoV-2 infected cells.
source: We therefore conclude that nucleocapsid and ORF3a are targets for ADNKA activity against SARS-CoV-2 infected cells, with membrane potentially also contributing.
evidence: This is the conclusion drawn from the antibody depletion and virus deletion experiments.

claim: Membrane potentially contributes to ADNKA activity against SARS-CoV-2 infected cells.
source: We therefore conclude that nucleocapsid and ORF3a are targets for ADNKA activity against SARS-CoV-2 infected cells, with membrane potentially also contributing.
evidence: This is inferred from the remaining ADNKA activity after spike, nucleocapsid, and ORF3a depletion/deletion.

claim: ELISA demonstrated effective depletion of spike antibodies from vaccine sera.
source: As with serum from naturally infected individuals, ELISA demonstrated effective depletion of spike antibodies (Figure 9A), which was accompanied by a marked loss of virus neutralisation activity (Figure 9B and C).
evidence: This is shown by ELISA in Figure 9A.

claim: Depletion of spike antibodies from vaccine sera was accompanied by a marked loss of virus neutralisation activity.
source: As with serum from naturally infected individuals, ELISA demonstrated effective depletion of spike antibodies (Figure 9A), which was accompanied by a marked loss of virus neutralisation activity (Figure 9B and C).
evidence: This is shown by neutralisation assays in Figures 9B and 9C.

claim: Vaccine sera only mediated weak ADNKA.
source: In functional NK assays, these sera only mediated weak ADNKA (Figure 9D and E) and, unlike sera from naturally infected individuals, ADNKA activity was abrogated following depletion of spike antibodies.
evidence: This is shown by ADNKA assays in Figures 9D and 9E.

claim: ADNKA activity from vaccine sera was abrogated following depletion of spike antibodies.
source: In functional NK assays, these sera only mediated weak ADNKA (Figure 9D and E) and, unlike sera from naturally infected individuals, ADNKA activity was abrogated following depletion of spike antibodies.
evidence: This is shown by comparing depleted and undepleted vaccine sera in Figures 9D and 9E.

claim: Vaccine mediated ADNKA was significantly weaker than responses seen following natural infection.
source: When we compared responses following natural infection or vaccination, vaccine mediated ADNKA was significantly weaker than responses seen following natural infection, and was not boosted following the second dose of the vaccine (Figure 9F).
evidence: This is shown by comparing vaccinated and naturally infected individuals in Figure 9F.

claim: Neutralisation activity of vaccine sera was dramatically increased following the second dose.
source: This was in stark contrast with the neutralisation activity of those same serum samples, which were dramatically increased following the second dose, with activity comparable to patients with severe COVID-19 disease (Figure 9G).
evidence: This is shown by comparing neutralisation after first and second doses in Figure 9G.

claim: Neutralisation activity after the second vaccine dose was comparable to patients with severe COVID-19 disease.
source: This was in stark contrast with the neutralisation activity of those same serum samples, which were dramatically increased following the second dose, with activity comparable to patients with severe COVID-19 disease (Figure 9G).
evidence: This is shown by comparing vaccinated individuals to naturally infected individuals in Figure 9G.

claim: Anti-spike antibodies can mediate ADNKA, but this activity is significantly weaker than responses seen during natural infection.
source: Thus, anti-spike antibodies can mediate ADNKA, but this activity is significantly weaker than responses seen during natural infection, which targets a broader repertoire of viral antigens.
evidence: This is the conclusion drawn from comparing vaccine and natural infection sera.

claim: ADNKA during natural infection targets a broader repertoire of viral antigens than vaccination.
source: Thus, anti-spike antibodies can mediate ADNKA, but this activity is significantly weaker than responses seen during natural infection, which targets a broader repertoire of viral antigens.
evidence: This is inferred from the antibody depletion experiments showing non-spike antigens contribute to ADNKA.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 remodelling of the plasma membrane leads to downregulation of multiple cell surface immune ligands involved with the interferon response, cytokine function, and NK activation.
source: We find that SARS-CoV-2 remodelling of the plasma membrane leads to the downregulation of multiple cell surface immune ligands involved with the interferon response, cytokine function, and NK activation.
evidence: This is the overall conclusion from the proteomic analysis.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 remodelling may enable the virus to evade numerous effector arms of the host immune system.
source: This may enable SARS-CoV-2 to evade numerous effector arms of the host immune system.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed downregulation of immune ligands.

claim: Shutdown of host transcription and translation is likely to play a broader role in the ability of the virus to establish initial infection than previously appreciated.
source: This provides an explanation for how small RNA viruses may be able to target the NK response without encoding the large repertoire of specific NK-evasins seen in the large DNA viruses (Patel et al., 2018; Berry et al., 2020), and indicates that shutdown of host transcription and translation is likely to play a broader role in the ability of the virus to establish initial infection than previously appreciated.
evidence: This is inferred from the mechanism of NK ligand downregulation via protein synthesis inhibition.

claim: ADNKA leads to significant degranulation and production of pro-inflammatory cytokines later in disease.
source: Later in disease, following the production of antibody, ADNKA leads to significant degranulation, and production of pro-inflammatory cytokines.
evidence: This is shown by functional NK cell assays with seropositive sera.

claim: Spike antibody is not responsible for the robust ADNKA which develops after natural infection.
source: Somewhat surprisingly, spike antibody is not responsible for the robust ADNKA which develops after natural infection, and only weak ADNKA is generated following spike vaccination.
evidence: This is the key finding from the antibody depletion experiments.

claim: Only weak ADNKA is generated following spike vaccination.
source: Somewhat surprisingly, spike antibody is not responsible for the robust ADNKA which develops after natural infection, and only weak ADNKA is generated following spike vaccination.
evidence: This is shown by comparing vaccine and natural infection sera in functional assays.

claim: Genetic variation in both viruses and their hosts affects the ability of viruses to modulate NK responses and influence pathogenesis.
source: Genetic variation in both viruses and their hosts affects the ability of viruses to modulate NK responses, and influence pathogenesis (Patel et al., 2018; Vietzen et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 appears to have evolved to antagonise NK activation by targeting the expression levels of multiple activating NK ligands.
source: SARS-CoV-2 appears to have evolved to antagonise NK activation by targeting the expression levels of multiple activating NK ligands.
evidence: This is the interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Targeting NKG2D ligands may enable the virus to impact additional effector mechanisms beyond just NK cells.
source: NKG2D is ubiquitously expressed on γδ cells and CD8+, as well as some CD4+, T-cells in addition to NK cells (Zingoni et al., 2018). Targeting NKG2D ligands may therefore enable the virus to impact additional effector mechanisms beyond just NK cells.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known expression pattern of NKG2D.

claim: MICA is particularly polymorphic with 100+ alleles.
source: Amongst NKG2D ligands, MICA is particularly polymorphic (100+alleles), A549 cells express MICA*001/004 (Seidel et al., 2015), while the truncated MICA*008 is the most common allele worldwide.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: A549 cells express MICA*001/004.
source: Amongst NKG2D ligands, MICA is particularly polymorphic (100+alleles), A549 cells express MICA*001/004 (Seidel et al., 2015), while the truncated MICA*008 is the most common allele worldwide.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Seidel et al., 2015.

claim: The truncated MICA*008 is the most common allele worldwide.
source: Amongst NKG2D ligands, MICA is particularly polymorphic (100+alleles), A549 cells express MICA*001/004 (Seidel et al., 2015), while the truncated MICA*008 is the most common allele worldwide.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MICA alleles.

claim: MICA diversity is largely driven by co-evolution of humans with virus infections.
source: This diversity is largely driven by co-evolution of humans with virus infections, and reflects the broad repertoire of viral immune-evasins (Zingoni et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: MICA variation has the potential to play a role in the extremely variable outcome of SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: MICA variation therefore has the potential to play a role in the extremely variable outcome of SARS-CoV-2 infection.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known importance of MICA in NK cell responses.

claim: NK cells stimulated with IL-12 and IL-15 were capable of controlling SARS-CoV-2 infection of VeroE6 or Calu3 cells.
source: A recent study demonstrated that NK cells stimulated with IL-12 and IL-15 were capable of controlling SARS-CoV-2 following infection of VeroE6 or Calu3 cells (Witkowski et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Witkowski et al., 2021.

claim: Strongly activating cytokines such as IL-12/IL-15 are likely capable of stimulating NK cells sufficiently to contribute to viral control despite viral evasion mechanisms.
source: Nevertheless, NK cell activity is heavily dependent on stimulation, and it is highly likely that strongly activating cytokines such as IL-12/IL-15 are capable of stimulating NK cells sufficiently to contribute to viral control despite viral evasion mechanisms.
evidence: This is speculation based on known NK cell biology.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 does not encode Fc receptors as ADNKA decoys.
source: Nor do infected cells bind human IgG from seronegative donors, indicating that it does not encode Fc receptors as ADNKA decoys.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that seronegative sera do not activate ADNKA.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 acts as an acute 'hit and run' virus, which has replicated and transmitted before host adaptive immunity develops.
source: These observations are consistent with SARS-CoV-2 acting as an acute 'hit and run' virus, which has replicated and transmitted before host adaptive immunity develops.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed lack of MHC-I downregulation and Fc receptor expression.

claim: A previous study demonstrated that SARS-CoV-2 downregulates HLA-A2 via ORF8.
source: A previous study has demonstrated that SARS-CoV-2 downregulates HLA-A2 via ORF8, which contrasts somewhat with our results (Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2021.

claim: The downregulation of HLA-A2 via ORF8 may indicate a HLA- or cell-type-specific effect.
source: This may indicate a HLA- or cell-type-specific effect, it will be interesting to determine whether coronaviruses evade innate and adaptive immunity in their original bat host, and whether this contributes to their persistence in that species.
evidence: This is speculation to reconcile the current findings with previous studies.

claim: Antibody-mediated activation of cellular immunity is a critical component of the protective immune response in animal models of vaccination and monoclonal antibody administration against SARS-CoV-2.
source: In animal models of vaccination (Gorman et al., 2021) and monoclonal antibody administration (Chan et al., 2020; Schäfer et al., 2021; Winkler et al., 2020; Suryadevara et al., 2021; Yamin et al., 2021) against SARS-CoV-2, antibody-mediated activation of cellular immunity is a critical component of the protective immune response.
evidence: This is supported by citations to animal studies.

claim: Inflammation dominates severe COVID-19 disease.
source: However, inflammation dominates severe COVID-19 disease (Horby et al., 2021b; Horby et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: The high levels of TNFα and IFNγ observed following ADNKA are likely to exacerbate disease in severe COVID-19.
source: The high levels of TNFα and IFNγ observed following ADNKA are likely to exacerbate disease under these circumstances.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed cytokine production and known role of inflammation in severe disease.

claim: TNFα and IFNγ correlate with severe COVID-19 disease.
source: In support of this, TNFα and IFNγ correlate with severe disease (Karki et al., 2021), and critically ill patients have a higher proportion of afucosylated antibodies that may promote a stronger ADCC response (Larsen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Critically ill patients have a higher proportion of afucosylated antibodies that may promote a stronger ADCC response.
source: In support of this, TNFα and IFNγ correlate with severe disease (Karki et al., 2021), and critically ill patients have a higher proportion of afucosylated antibodies that may promote a stronger ADCC response (Larsen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Larsen et al., 2021.

claim: ADCC can potentially contribute to both protection and immunopathology.
source: Given that ADCC can potentially contribute to both protection and immunopathology, it is important to understand what determines the magnitude and quality of the ADCC response.
evidence: This is inferred from the dual role of inflammation in viral control and disease.

claim: Non-structural accessory proteins were more potent ADCC targets than entry glycoproteins during HCMV infection.
source: Although antibodies targeting these antigens can clearly bind infected cells, using similar approaches to the present study we recently showed that non-structural accessory proteins were more potent ADCC targets during HCMV infection (Vlahava et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Monoclonal anti-spike antibodies were only effective at activating Fc-mediated control of infection in animal models following engineering to enhance activity.
source: In support of this data, monoclonal anti-spike antibodies were only effective at activating Fc-mediated control of infection in animal models following engineering to enhance activity (Beaudoin-Bussières et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Beaudoin-Bussières et al., 2021.

claim: The differential ability of spike mAbs to activate ADNKA may result from differential post-translational modifications of spike between transfected and infected cells.
source: Numerous spike mAbs were capable of potently activating ADNKA against transfected cells, but failed to stimulate NK cells in the presence of infected cells; this may result from differential post-translational modifications of spike between these contexts, the fact that the reduction in activating NK ligands as a result of infection alters the threshold for activation through ADNKA, or the fact that viral CPE affects the formation of an immunological synapse (Stanton et al., 2014).
evidence: This is speculation to explain the observed differences.

claim: The reduction in activating NK ligands as a result of infection may alter the threshold for activation through ADNKA.
source: Numerous spike mAbs were capable of potently activating ADNKA against transfected cells, but failed to stimulate NK cells in the presence of infected cells; this may result from differential post-translational modifications of spike between these contexts, the fact that the reduction in activating NK ligands as a result of infection alters the threshold for activation through ADNKA, or the fact that viral CPE affects the formation of an immunological synapse (Stanton et al., 2014).
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed NK ligand downregulation.

claim: Viral CPE may affect the formation of an immunological synapse.
source: Numerous spike mAbs were capable of potently activating ADNKA against transfected cells, but failed to stimulate NK cells in the presence of infected cells; this may result from differential post-translational modifications of spike between these contexts, the fact that the reduction in activating NK ligands as a result of infection alters the threshold for activation through ADNKA, or the fact that viral CPE affects the formation of an immunological synapse (Stanton et al., 2014).
